claim: RAS family of proteins is amongst the most highly mutated in human cancers.
source: The RAS family of proteins is amongst the most highly mutated in human cancers and has so far eluded drug therapy.
evidence: This is supported by citations to established literature and is part of scientific consensus in the field.

claim: RAS has so far eluded drug therapy.
source: The RAS family of proteins is amongst the most highly mutated in human cancers and has so far eluded drug therapy.
evidence: This statement reflects the established knowledge in the field at the time of writing.

claim: A robust set of BRET-based RAS biosensors has been developed that enable monitoring of RAS-effector interaction inhibition in living cells.
source: Here, we have developed a robust set of bioluminescence resonance energy transfer (BRET)-based RAS biosensors that enable monitoring of RAS-effector interaction inhibition in living cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The RAS biosensors include KRAS, HRAS and NRAS.
source: These include KRAS, HRAS and NRAS and a variety of different mutations that mirror those found in human cancers with the major RAS effectors such as CRAF, PI3K and RALGDS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing the construction and testing of these biosensors.

claim: The RAS biosensors include a variety of different mutations that mirror those found in human cancers.
source: These include KRAS, HRAS and NRAS and a variety of different mutations that mirror those found in human cancers with the major RAS effectors such as CRAF, PI3K and RALGDS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and design choices based on known cancer mutations.

claim: The RAS biosensors work with major RAS effectors such as CRAF, PI3K and RALGDS.
source: These include KRAS, HRAS and NRAS and a variety of different mutations that mirror those found in human cancers with the major RAS effectors such as CRAF, PI3K and RALGDS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing interactions with these effectors.

claim: A RAS-binding compound is a potent pan-RAS-effector interactions inhibitor in cells.
source: We highlighted the utility of these RAS biosensors by showing a RAS-binding compound is a potent pan-RAS-effector interactions inhibitor in cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BRET assays and western blots.

claim: Mutation in RAS proteins can be found in approximately 30% of all human tumors.
source: Mutation in RAS proteins can be found in approximately 30% of all human tumors (Downward, 2003; Prior et al., 2012) (http://cancer.sanger.ac.uk/cosmic) prompting interest in the discovery of anti-RAS therapeutics.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and database references.

claim: There are still no RAS-targeted drugs currently available in the clinic.
source: However, there are still no RAS-targeted drugs currently available in the clinic even though such molecules could prove widely efficacious in many human cancers as front-line drugs for therapy.
evidence: This reflects the state of the field at the time of writing.

claim: Pancreatic cancer contains a high proportion of KRAS mutations.
source: Some forms of cancer, like pancreatic cancer, present late and are difficult therefore to treat (Kleeff et al., 2016) but these contain a high proportion of KRAS mutations and are thus potentially susceptible to RAS-binding drugs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RAS has been regarded as undruggable partly because so far attempts to interfere with the protein have not been efficacious.
source: RAS has been regarded as undruggable partly because so far attempts to interfere with the protein have not been efficacious (Cox et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RAS is a membrane-bound small GTPase switching between an inactive GDP-bound state and an active GTP-bound state.
source: RAS is a membrane-bound small GTPase switching between an inactive GDP-bound state and an active GTP-bound state.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RAS protein function.

claim: RAS signaling to the cell nucleus occurs after interaction of RAS-GTP with its effectors to trigger the activation of downstream signaling pathways.
source: RAS signaling to the cell nucleus occurs after interaction of RAS-GTP with its effectors to trigger the activation of downstream signaling pathways.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RAS signaling.

claim: RAS activation promotes cell survival and cell proliferation via gene modulation.
source: This activation thereby promotes cell survival and cell proliferation (Wennerberg et al., 2005) via gene modulation so that the blockade of mutant RAS signaling in tumors cells is an attractive therapeutic option.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The effectiveness of orthosteric RAS-effector PPI inhibition was shown using intracellular antibodies.
source: However, the effectiveness of the orthosteric RAS-effector PPI inhibition was shown using intracellular antibodies (Tanaka and Rabbitts, 2003; Tanaka et al., 2007) (herein called macrodrugs (Tanaka and Rabbitts, 2008) to distinguish them from conventional small molecule drugs) and a single domain intracellular antibody that blocks effector interaction sites of RAS-GTP.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: PPI inhibition can prevent tumor growth in xenograft models and tumor initiation in a transgenic mouse model.
source: This PPI inhibition can prevent tumor growth in xenograft models and tumor initiation in a transgenic mouse model (Tanaka and Rabbitts, 2010; Tanaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: DARPins have been shown to be effective in interfering with RAS PPIs.
source: Other macrodrugs, such as DARPins (Guillard et al., 2017), have also been shown to be effective in interfering with RAS PPIs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RAS was regarded as a protein without any pockets suitable for small molecule interactions.
source: Moreover, for many years, RAS was regarded as a protein without any pockets suitable for small molecule interactions (McCormick, 2016) but recent studies have described compounds that are able to bind RAS-associated pockets (Gentile et al., 2017; Lito et al., 2016; Maurer et al., 2012; Ostrem et al., 2013; Patricelli et al., 2016; Shima et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2012; Waldmann et al., 2004; Welsch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Recent studies have described compounds that are able to bind RAS-associated pockets.
source: Moreover, for many years, RAS was regarded as a protein without any pockets suitable for small molecule interactions (McCormick, 2016) but recent studies have described compounds that are able to bind RAS-associated pockets (Gentile et al., 2017; Lito et al., 2016; Maurer et al., 2012; Ostrem et al., 2013; Patricelli et al., 2016; Shima et al., 2013; Sun et al., 2012; Waldmann et al., 2004; Welsch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Most current RAS inhibitors have been selected and identified through in vitro techniques.
source: Most of the current RAS inhibitors have been selected and identified through in vitro techniques (Ostrem et al., 2013; Trinh et al., 2016; Upadhyaya et al., 2015; Welsch et al., 2017) but cell-based assay technologies are needed to assess initial hits for efficacy before hit to lead development is undertaken.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Cell-based assay technologies are needed to assess initial hits for efficacy before hit to lead development is undertaken.
source: Most of the current RAS inhibitors have been selected and identified through in vitro techniques (Ostrem et al., 2013; Trinh et al., 2016; Upadhyaya et al., 2015; Welsch et al., 2017) but cell-based assay technologies are needed to assess initial hits for efficacy before hit to lead development is undertaken.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of drug development processes.

claim: A robust cell-based assay provides insights into the behavior of compounds in physiological conditions, including cell permeability, stability and potency in the cellular complexity of a whole cell.
source: Indeed, a robust cell-based assay is a mandatory step in any drug discovery programme, as it provides insights into the behavior of compounds in physiological conditions, including cell permeability, stability and potency in the cellular complexity of a whole cell.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of drug development processes.

claim: The intracellular localization of BRET donor RAS proteins was recapitulated by expressing the full-length proteins including the CAAX box.
source: The intracellular localization of BRET donor RAS proteins was recapitulated by expressing the full-length proteins including the CAAX box, which is the farnesylation site for trafficking to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is supported by experimental design and established knowledge of RAS localization.

claim: The CAAX box is the farnesylation site for trafficking to the plasma membrane.
source: The intracellular localization of BRET donor RAS proteins was recapitulated by expressing the full-length proteins including the CAAX box, which is the farnesylation site for trafficking to the plasma membrane.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about RAS protein localization.

claim: A higher BRET signal was observed with a (GGGS)3 linker between RLuc8-KRASG12D construct.
source: For our study, we observed a higher BRET signal with a (GGGS)3 linker between RLuc8-KRASG12D construct, a (GGGS)3 linker between the CRAF RBD-GFP2 molecule and a (GGGS)2 linker between iDAb RAS-GFP2 construct (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: A higher BRET signal was observed with a (GGGS)3 linker between the CRAF RBD-GFP2 molecule.
source: For our study, we observed a higher BRET signal with a (GGGS)3 linker between RLuc8-KRASG12D construct, a (GGGS)3 linker between the CRAF RBD-GFP2 molecule and a (GGGS)2 linker between iDAb RAS-GFP2 construct (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: A higher BRET signal was observed with a (GGGS)2 linker between iDAb RAS-GFP2 construct.
source: For our study, we observed a higher BRET signal with a (GGGS)3 linker between RLuc8-KRASG12D construct, a (GGGS)3 linker between the CRAF RBD-GFP2 molecule and a (GGGS)2 linker between iDAb RAS-GFP2 construct (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: If an interaction occurs between RAS and a partner-GFP2 fusion, bringing the RLuc8 and GFP2 within 100 Å, an energy transfer occurs from the RLuc8-RAS donor to the GFP2 acceptor and a BRET2 signal is achieved.
source: If an interaction occurs between RAS and a partner-GFP2 fusion, bringing the RLuc8 and GFP2 within 100 Å, an energy transfer occurs from the RLuc8-RAS donor to the GFP2 acceptor and a BRET2 signal is achieved (Figure 1A, middle panel).
evidence: This is based on established BRET methodology and experimental design.

claim: Inhibitors of the donor-acceptor molecule interaction will decrease the BRET signal whilst maintaining the RLuc8 bioluminescence and GFP2 fluorescence signals.
source: Inhibitors of the donor-acceptor molecule interaction will decrease the BRET signal whilst maintaining the RLuc8 bioluminescence and GFP2 fluorescence signals (Figure 1A, right hand panel).
evidence: This is based on established BRET methodology and experimental design.

claim: All of the effector domains were found to interact specifically with KRASG12D since the BRET signal reached a donor saturation level.
source: All of the effector domains were found to interact specifically with KRASG12D since the BRET signal reached a donor saturation level (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The dominant negative mutant KRASS17N does not interact with the effectors.
source: To further characterize this BRET2 system, we used the dominant negative mutant KRASS17N, which does not interact with the effectors (Cool et al., 1999; Nassar et al., 2010; van den Berghe et al., 1997), as a donor.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and experimental data.

claim: The BRET signal increased linearly with the concentration of acceptor for all the RAS binding domains with KRASS17N.
source: We found that the BRET signal increased linearly with the concentration of acceptor for all the RAS binding domains. This result is typical of non-specific interactions (Mercier et al., 2002), confirming the S17N mutant does not interact with the effectors and supports the sensitivity of this system (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to published literature on BRET methodology.

claim: iDAb RAS interacts with mutant KRAS on the switch regions.
source: We initially characterized the biosensor pairs with the iDAb RAS that is known to interact with mutant KRAS on the switch regions (Tanaka et al., 2007), compared with a non-relevant anti-LMO2 iDAb (Sewell et al., 2014; Tanaka et al., 2011) that was designated as iDAb control in this study (herein called iDAb Ctl).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Introduction of mutations in the three CDRs of the iDAb RAS to generate a dematured iDAb RAS reduced its affinity towards RAS-GTP from 6.2 nM to ~1 μM affinity.
source: Introduction of mutations in the three CDRs of the iDAb RAS to generate a dematured iDAb RAS (iDAbdm RAS), was shown to reduce its affinity towards RAS-GTP from 6.2 nM to ~1 μM affinity (Assi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: iDAb RAS, but not the control, drastically decreased the BRET ratio of all the interactions tested.
source: This competition showed that iDAb RAS, but not the control, drastically decreased the BRET ratio of all the interactions tested (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: Compound 3344 binds to KRASG12V with an affinity of 126 nM using 1H Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) NMR.
source: We have identified compounds that bind to KRAS using in vitro screening and one compound 3344 (chemical structure and 1-D NMR characterization shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C) binds to KRASG12V with an affinity of 126 nM using 1H Carr-Purcell-Meiboom-Gill (CPMG) NMR (Baldwin and Kay, 2009) (data are shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure and citation to the NMR method.

claim: In vitro competition studies of 3344 binding to KRASG12V in waterLOGSY NMR show the anti-RAS scFv inhibits 3344 binding to KRAS.
source: In vitro competition studies of 3344 binding to KRASG12V in waterLOGSY NMR show the anti-RAS scFv inhibits 3344 binding to KRAS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: A dose response reduction in BRET signal was observed for the assays with compound 3344 but not with the Abd-2.
source: We observed a dose response reduction in BRET signal for the assays with compound 3344 but not with the Abd-2 indicating that only 3344 interferes with the RAS-effector PPI (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: 3344 only interferes, in a dose response, with KRASG12D/iDAbdm RAS-induced BRET without affecting the expression of the biosensors.
source: Abd-2 has no effect on any of these assays while 3344 only interferes, in a dose response, with KRASG12D/iDAbdm RAS-induced BRET without affecting the expression of the biosensors (Figure 1—figure supplement 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The S257L mutation increases ERK phosphorylation.
source: To reduce this limitation, we developed an optimized RAS biosensor of the full-length CRAFS257L mutant (herein named CRAFFL) since the S257L mutation increases ERK phosphorylation (Razzaque et al., 2007) and because we found that CRAFFL interacts with KRASG12D but not with KRASS17N (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature and experimental data.

claim: CRAFFL interacts with KRASG12D but not with KRASS17N.
source: To reduce this limitation, we developed an optimized RAS biosensor of the full-length CRAFS257L mutant (herein named CRAFFL) since the S257L mutation increases ERK phosphorylation (Razzaque et al., 2007) and because we found that CRAFFL interacts with KRASG12D but not with KRASS17N (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: iDAb RAS impedes the BRET2 signal due to the binding of CRAFFL with KRASG12D, in a dose response mode.
source: We performed a competition assay with the iDAb RAS confirming that it impedes the BRET2 signal due to the binding of CRAFFL with KRASG12D, in a dose response mode, whereas the iDAb control had no effect (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: iDAb RAS inhibition significantly decreased the phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 kinases.
source: In addition, iDAb RAS inhibition significantly decreased the phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 kinases (Figure 2B shows western blot data, quantitated in Figure 2C), confirming results affecting endogenous ERK phosphorylation by iDAb RAS interaction with RAS (Tanaka and Rabbitts, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures and citation to published literature.

claim: Compound 3344 induces a dose-dependent decrease of MEK and ERK kinase phosphorylation.
source: This induces a dose-dependent decrease of MEK and ERK kinase phosphorylation (E) after cells expressing the KRASG12D/CRAFFL biosensor pair were treated 20 hr with DMSO, 10 and 20 μM of Abd-2 and 3344 compounds or not treated (untreated lane).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: 3344 also significantly inhibited MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 phosphorylation whilst Abd-2 did not.
source: Western blots using anti-pMEK and anti-pERK showed that 3344 also significantly inhibited MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 phosphorylation whilst Abd-2 did not (Figure 2E, quantified in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Some compounds have been previously characterized that bind selectively on the cysteine of KRASG12C mutant.
source: Some compounds have been previously characterized that bind selectively on the cysteine of KRASG12C mutant (Lito et al., 2016; Ostrem et al., 2013; Patricelli et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Analysis of the BRET2 signals from interaction of KRASG12A, KRASG12C, KRASG12V and KRASG12R with CRAFFL showed a dose response effect of compound 3344 but not Abd-2.
source: Analysis of the BRET2 signals from interaction of KRASG12A, KRASG12C, KRASG12V and KRASG12R with CRAFFL showed a dose response effect of compound 3344 but not Abd-2 (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The compound disrupts mutant KRAS/CRAFFL interaction in cells.
source: Therefore, using this new set of validated RAS biosensors, we show that the compound disrupts mutant KRAS/CRAFFL interaction in cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BRET assays.

claim: Disruption of KRAS/CRAFFL interaction leads to inhibition of the RAF/MEK/ERK downstream signaling pathway.
source: In turn, this leads to inhibition of the RAF/MEK/ERK downstream signaling pathway (that emanates from the transfected protein expression).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from western blots showing reduced phosphorylation.

claim: EGF treatment brings KRASWT and CRAFFL fusion proteins in a closer proximity and enhances the number of KRASWT/CRAFFL dimers.
source: EGF treatment brings KRASWT and CRAFFL fusion proteins in a closer proximity and enhances the number of KRASWT/CRAFFL dimers because the BRETmax value increases from 4.02 to 10.01 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: A dose response inhibition of the BRET2 signal was observed with iDAb RAS, but not iDAb control.
source: A dose response inhibition of the BRET2 signal was observed with iDAb RAS, but not iDAb control (Figure 3A), which correlated with the reduction of pMEK1/2 and pERK1/2 detected by western blots (Figure 3B and quantified in Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Compound 3344 inhibits KRASWT/CRAFFL interaction after EGF treatment in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The effect on BRET2 signal of compounds Abd-2 (grey bars) and 3344 (black bars) on KRASWT/CRAFFL interaction after EGF treatment in a BRET competition experiment is shown in panel D.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: 3344 prevents the phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 kinases in KRASWT/CRAFFL biosensor after EGF stimulation.
source: Compound 3344 inhibits this interaction in a dose-response manner (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) and prevents the phosphorylation of MEK1/2 and ERK1/2 kinases (Figure 3E, quantified in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Co-expression of the p85α regulatory subunit with PI3KαFL-GFP2 was required to obtain detectable, specific and optimized BRET signal from interaction of KRASG12D and PI3KαFL.
source: In this case, we required a tripartite system as we observed that co-expression of the p85α regulatory subunit with PI3KαFL-GFP2 was required to obtain detectable, specific and optimized BRET signal from interaction of KRASG12D and PI3KαFL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: iDAb RAS impaired KRASG12D/PI3KαFL interaction in a dose-dependent manner.
source: We validated the BRET biosensor by showing that the iDAb RAS impaired that interaction in a dose-dependent manner, whereas the iDAb control did not (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: iDAb RAS causes a dose response reduction of phosphorylation of the downstream biomarker AKT at Ser473.
source: Western blot analysis showed some reduction in PI3K and RAS proteins, specifically concordant with expression of the iDAb RAS (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) and there was also a dose response reduction of phosphorylation of the downstream biomarker AKT at Ser473 (Figure 4B and quantified in Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: 3344 interferes with the KRASG12D/PI3KαFL interaction.
source: Implementing the same biosensor assay treated with the compound 3344 for 3 or 20 hr, we confirmed this compound interferes with the KRASG12D/PI3KαFL interaction (Figure 4D–F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F) without loss of protein (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: 3344 affects RAS-PI3K interaction and AKT phosphorylation.
source: Conversely, 3344 does affect RAS-PI3K interaction and AKT phosphorylation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BRET assays and western blots.

claim: 3344 inhibits RAS-PI3Kα PPI and thus signaling through AKT.
source: 3344 inhibits RAS-PI3Kα PPI and thus signaling through AKT.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BRET assays and western blots.

claim: KRAS, NRAS and HRAS family members are conserved proteins that have an almost identical amino-acid domain (G domain) from residues 1–166 but a C-terminal hypervariable domain.
source: The KRAS, NRAS and HRAS family members are conserved proteins that have an almost identical amino-acid domain (G domain) from residues 1–166 but a C-terminal hypervariable domain (Wennerberg et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: RLuc8-NRASQ61H and RLuc8-HRASG12V proteins interact and reach plateau BRET signals with GFP2-CRAFFL.
source: Titration of the RAS donor and CRAFFL acceptor proteins show that the RLuc8-NRASQ61H and RLuc8-HRASG12V proteins interact and reach plateau BRET signals with GFP2-CRAFFL (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure.

claim: The BRET2 signal is diminished by increasing levels of the iDAb RAS but not the iDAb control for NRAS and HRAS biosensors.
source: Furthermore, the BRET2 signal is diminished by increasing levels of the iDAb RAS but not the iDAb control (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B–D) as expected from the analysis of the effects of the anti-RAS intracellular antibody (Tanaka and Rabbitts, 2010; Tanaka et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figure and citations to published literature.

claim: The compound 3344 disturbs the BRET2 signal in a dose-response manner in all NRAS and HRAS interactions with effectors.
source: While the low-affinity Abd-2 compound does not interfere with the BRET signal in any of the NRAS and HRAS BRET assays using either effector RBDs (Figure 5A,B) or full-length CRAF (Figure 5C,D), the compound 3344 disturbs the BRET2 signal in a dose-response manner in all these RAS interactions (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1E,F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: The BRET-based RAS biosensors characterization of 3344 shows this compound as a pan-RAS-effector interactions inhibitor that binds KRAS, NRAS and HRAS.
source: Therefore, the BRET-based RAS biosensors characterization of 3344 shows this compound as a pan-RAS-effector interactions inhibitor that binds KRAS, NRAS and HRAS.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BRET assays with multiple RAS isoforms.

claim: 3344 binds to KRAS in a previously identified pocket close to the switch regions where the effectors interact with RAS.
source: The mechanism of the interaction inhibition was corroborated by X-ray crystallography of KRASQ61H soaked with compound 3344. Figure 6A shows that 3344 binds to KRAS in a previously identified pocket (Maurer et al., 2012; Sun et al., 2012) close to the switch regions where the effectors interact with RAS (Table 1 has the refinement statistics for the X-ray data).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray crystallography data and citations to published literature.

claim: Parts of 3344 would overlap with the bound effector structures, suggesting that the competition effect of 3344 can be explained by straightforward steric hindrance.
source: The superimposition of the structures of three RAS-effector protein complexes with the structure of KRAS-3344 complex shows that parts of 3344 would overlap with the bound effector structures, suggesting that the competition effect of 3344 can be explained by straightforward steric hindrance (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis and inference from the crystallography data.

claim: 3344 decreases EGF-induced pAKT and pERK1/2 abundance in both DLD-1 and H358 cell types with an observed IC50 of ~5–10 μM.
source: 3344 decreases EGF-induced pAKT and pERK1/2 abundance in both cell types with an observed IC50 of ~5–10 μM without any change in the total levels of AKT or ERK1/2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from western blots of cancer cell lines.

claim: 3344 can interfere with endogenous RAS signaling in human cancer cell lines.
source: Therefore, 3344 can interfere with endogenous RAS signaling in human cancer cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cancer cell line assays.

claim: The mechanism of inhibition of the biomarkers in the tumor cell assay is direct interference of RAS-effector PPI by 3344.
source: As our BRET2 results show direct interference of RAS-effector PPI by 3344, we conclude that this is the mechanism of inhibition of the biomarkers in the tumor cell assay.
evidence: This is based on inference from the BRET data and tumor cell assay results.

claim: BRET-based biosensors have been successfully used to discover and characterize small molecules inhibitors.
source: BRET-based biosensors have been successfully used to discover and characterize small molecules inhibitors (Beautrait et al., 2017; Corbel et al., 2011; Lavoie et al., 2013; Mazars and Fåhraeus, 2010; Robinson et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The RAS biosensors allow the monitoring of RAS-effector interactions and the assessment of RAS PPI inhibition by a macrodrug (iDAb RAS) and 3344 in living cells.
source: This toolbox allows the monitoring of RAS-effector interactions and the assessment of RAS PPI inhibition by a macrodrug (iDAb RAS) and 3344, a new anti-RAS small molecule derived from an intracellular antibody fragment, in living cells.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BRET assays.

claim: When the full-length biosensors were used, RAS PPI inhibition could be coupled to the signaling effects.
source: Furthermore, when the full-length biosensors were used, we could couple the RAS PPI inhibition to the signaling effects, thereby providing additional insights into the behavior of RAS inhibitors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BRET assays and western blots.

claim: The inhibition of RAS PPI by 3344 in cells was demonstrated by the RAS biosensors toolbox and validated by X-ray crystallography.
source: The inhibition of RAS PPI by 3344 in cells was demonstrated by the RAS biosensors toolbox and validated by X-ray crystallography.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BRET assays and crystallography.

claim: 3344 binds to a hydrophobic pocket near to the effector-binding switch regions of RAS.
source: 3344 binds to a hydrophobic pocket near to the effector-binding switch regions of RAS (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by X-ray crystallography data.

claim: 3344 does not make direct contact with the switch regions.
source: Whereas 3344 does not make direct contact with the switch regions, the BRET data show that the binding geometry and potency of 3344 is sufficient to interfere with the interaction of RAS-effector molecules that bind close to the 3344 site.
evidence: This is based on structural analysis from crystallography and BRET data.

claim: The RAS biosensors provide a direct and quantitative measurement of the PPI interference with inhibitors.
source: It provides a direct and quantitative measurement of the PPI interference with inhibitors (i.e. small molecules or macrodrugs), which could allow the comparison of different compounds (e.g. for structure-activity-relationship studies) or macrodrugs and therefore the selection of more potent inhibitors.
evidence: This is based on the experimental design and capabilities of the BRET assay.

claim: 3344 prevents endogenous RAS-dependent signaling in two different human tumor cell lines at a lower concentration (IC50 around 5 μM) than in the BRET assay with observed IC50 around 20 μM.
source: Nonetheless, 3344 prevents endogenous RAS-dependent signaling in two different human tumor cell lines at a lower concentration (IC50 around 5 μM) (Figure 6C,D) than in the BRET assay with observed IC50 around 20 μM.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from cancer cell lines and BRET assays.

claim: The difference in IC50 between BRET assay and tumor cell assay probably reflects the expression levels of the target proteins in the two assays.
source: This difference probably reflects the expression levels of the target proteins in the two assays, where the BRET2 assay relies on transient transfection.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental design differences.

claim: The overexpression in HEK293T cells probably produces higher amount of mutant RAS/effector proteins than the endogenous counterparts in cancer cells.
source: Indeed, the overexpression in HEK293T cells probably produces higher amount of mutant RAS/effector proteins than the endogenous counterparts in cancer cells.
evidence: This is based on inference from the experimental design.

claim: It might be more difficult to quantitatively inhibit the exogenous RAS/effector interaction than the endogenous one with 3344 compound.
source: Therefore, it might be more difficult to quantitatively inhibit the exogenous RAS/effector interaction than the endogenous one with 3344 compound.
evidence: This is based on inference from the IC50 differences observed.

claim: The biosensors allowed a recapitulation of the published features of the iDAb RAS intracellular single domain antibody.
source: Another advantage of this toolbox has been shown by using the iDAb RAS as an acceptor within the RAS biosensors allowing a recapitulation of the published features of this intracellular single domain antibody.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from BRET assays and citations to published literature.

claim: Studies suggested that isoform and residue- or codon-specific RAS mutants show differences in their ability to engage effectors and signaling properties.
source: Indeed, studies suggested that isoform and residue- or codon-specific RAS mutants show differences in their ability to engage effectors and signaling properties (Hunter et al., 2015; Nakhaeizadeh et al., 2016; Yan et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: RAS biosensors could be a methodology to decipher RAS isoform/mutant properties in cells.
source: Accordingly, RAS biosensors could also be a methodology to decipher RAS isoform/mutant properties in cells.
evidence: This is based on speculation about potential applications of the biosensors.

claim: The toolbox is an available resource for RAS-drug development programmes.
source: Our toolbox is an available resource for RAS-drug development programmes, and more generally for the RAS community, since our results demonstrate the possibility of using these RAS biosensors as a generic method to characterize cell-potent RAS-binding compounds or RAS-binding macrodrugs.
evidence: This is based on the demonstrated utility of the biosensors.

claim: The BRET2 biosensor system could be used for direct screens of PPI inhibitors with libraries of compounds.
source: The BRET2 biosensor system could also be used for direct screens of PPI inhibitors with libraries of compounds.
evidence: This is based on speculation about potential applications of the biosensors.

claim: Reduction of affinity (dematuration) from a tool initially used for target validation can be achieved to make a screening tool.
source: This provides a further use of intracellular domain antibodies where reduction of affinity (dematuration) from a tool initially used for target validation, can be achieved to make a screening tool.
evidence: This is based on the demonstrated use of dematured iDAb in the study.

claim: The method is an approach that is transferable to other PPI situations required for drug development programmes in cancer or any other clinical indication.
source: Thus, the method is an approach that is transferable to other PPI situations required for drug development programmes in cancer or any other clinical indication.
evidence: This is based on speculation about the broader applicability of the method.

claim: The KRAS mutations in the two human cancer cell lines were confirmed as KRASG13D in DLD-1 and KRASG12C in H358.
source: The KRAS mutations in the two human cancer cell lines were confirmed as KRASG13D in DLD-1 and KRASG12C in H358.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from sequencing.
